sections.title: SEO for software and technology companies
sections.text: Software buyers don't always search for a product by name. Sometimes they start with a problem, a use case, a comparison between two solutions, or a check that an integration exists with a system they already use. We organize your product pages around these questions, clearly explain the features, limitations and benefits your company confirms, and then make it easy to start a trial or request a demo.

sections.text: A business owner may not know your product's name, but they're searching for a way to manage inventory or connect sales to accounting. We write pages for the use cases your product actually serves, then link them to the relevant features and integrations. Your main product page explains who uses it, what it does and where its scope ends, instead of a long list of technical terms that don't answer the buyer's question.

sections.label: Verified features & integrations
sections.title: Verify every feature and integration before publishing
sections.text: Integration and comparison pages can help buyers choose, but they need details confirmed by the technical team. When comparing alternatives, we separate verified facts from marketing opinion. We don't create dozens of pages by just swapping in a competitor's name, and we never promise a feature that isn't available.

items.text: We track each of these steps separately, and measure the number of qualified requests when sales data is available.
This shows which topics attract attention and which pages actually help start a sales conversation.

items.question: Do we need a page for every integration?
items.answer: For verified integrations that customers search for and that have different setup details, yes. We don't create a page for an integration that doesn't exist or whose workings aren't known.

items.question: What's the difference between a feature page and a use-case page?
items.answer: A feature page explains what the product does, while a use-case page explains the problem it solves for a specific type of customer. The use-case page is usually closer to how people search.

items.question: When is a comparison page useful?
items.answer: When there are verifiable facts about the differences, and the page is written neutrally, without attacking the competitor or claiming features that aren't available.

items.question: Which metric do you track?
items.answer: Qualified demo and trial requests coming from search, not general traffic alone.
